questions.q: When your laptop asks a recursive resolver to look up www.example.com, what does the resolver ask first?
options: The authoritative server for example.com directly
A root server, which points it toward the right TLD server
Another resolver chosen at random
The TXT record for the domain
questions.explain: Unless the answer is already cached, the resolver starts at a root server, which points it to the TLD server (.com), which points it to the authoritative server for example.com.

questions.q: What does a CNAME record actually do?
options: Maps a name directly to an IPv4 address
Points one name to another name, which must eventually resolve to an A or AAAA record
Lists which mail server handles email for the domain
Stores free-form text like SPF/DKIM data
questions.explain: A CNAME is an alias — the resolver has to follow it to another name, and keep following until it reaches an actual A or AAAA record.

questions.q: In nslookup output, what does "Non-authoritative answer" mean?
options: The answer is incorrect and should not be trusted
The answer came from the resolver's cache rather than fresh from the domain's own authoritative server
The domain has no authoritative server configured
DNSSEC validation failed
questions.explain: It simply means the resolver answered from its cache instead of querying example.com's authoritative server fresh for that lookup.

questions.q: What does a record's TTL control?
options: How many IP addresses a domain can have
How long, in seconds, a resolver may cache that record before it has to re-check it with the authoritative server
How fast the domain's web server responds
Whether the record is an A record or a CNAME
questions.explain: TTL (time to live) is the caching window — a low TTL means changes show up faster everywhere, at the cost of more queries hitting the authoritative server.

questions.q: Which record type would you check to find out which mail server handles email for a domain?
options: A record
NS record
MX record
CNAME record
questions.explain: MX (mail exchange) records list which mail server(s) handle a domain's email, and in what priority order.
